title: The Next Global Order
dek: Power, technology, and a more multipolar world.
questions: Who writes the rules when no single power can?
Is neutrality a position or a strategy?
Where does technology fit in statecraft?

chapters.title: The end of the single center

transcript.text: We talk about a “global order” as if someone designed it. David, did anyone?
Someone designed parts of it, after 1945. What we have now is mostly the residue of those designs, plus a great deal of improvisation.
From Beirut it never looked like order. It looked like whose rules apply on which day.
So is the change we’re living through a collapse, or just more people noticing?
Both. The architecture is still standing, but fewer countries believe it was built with them in mind.
And technology is now where the rules actually get written: chips, cables, platforms.
Which brings us to the middle. Is choosing not to choose a strategy?
It’s the oldest strategy there is. The question is whether it can be coordinated.

title: Bridging AI and Opportunity
dek: Innovation, work, and who the dividend is really for.
questions: Who is AI’s opportunity actually for?
Can policy move at the speed of deployment?

transcript.text: Maya, when people say AI will create opportunity, I always want to ask: for whom?
That’s the right question, and it’s usually asked too late — after the systems are deployed.
Policy tends to arrive after the market has already decided who benefits.
Which is why I spend more time on procurement than on principles. Who buys the system shapes who it serves.
Ravi, you invest in this. Does the money care about access?
Money cares about returns. Access becomes interesting when it becomes a market.

title: Designing Belonging
dek: On thresholds, stoops, and the feeling of being expected.
questions: Can a place make you feel expected?
What do generous cities have in common?

transcript.text: Elena, you’ve written that belonging is the feeling of being expected. Say more.
It’s walking into a room and realizing someone saved you a seat. Not welcomed — expected.
Cities can do that too. A bench, a wide stoop, a café that doesn’t hurry you.
So you can design for it?
You can design against it very easily. Designing for it takes more humility.
The best places are generous to strangers. That’s where belonging starts.

title: Sport, Identity and Agency
dek: Who you are when the whistle stops.
questions: What happens to identity when a career ends?
How do young athletes find a voice?

chapters.title: Who you are when you stop

transcript.text: Lucas, what happens to identity when the career ends?
You find out how much of you was the jersey. For me, a lot.
With young athletes I see the opposite risk — the sport becomes the only place they’re allowed to be someone.
So agency is learning to be someone off the pitch too.
Agency is having a voice before you have a title.
The scoreboard resets. The people you became with your team — that stays.

title: Cities, People and Belonging
questions: What does a planner see that the rest of us miss?
Is informal the same as disorder?

transcript.text: Aisha, what does a planner see that the rest of us walk past?
Where people actually sit. Where they wait. The city tells you what it needs if you watch long enough.
Informal markets are often called chaos. They’re usually the most finely tuned systems in the city.
Then what’s the planner’s job?
Not to replace them. To plan with the people already doing the work.

title: AI, Work and the Human Edge
dek: What robots teach us about the work worth keeping.
questions: Is automation replacement or negotiation?
What is the human edge?

transcript.text: Hiro, you build robots. What do people get wrong about them?
They imagine replacement. What I see is negotiation — the robot takes a task, the person redefines the job.
Machines are still poor at the unexpected. A child runs into the aisle; the person adapts, the robot stops.
So the human edge is improvisation?
Improvisation and responsibility. Someone has to own the outcome.

title: Africa’s Next Chapter
dek: The youngest continent, its cities, and its choices.
questions: Who gets to tell the story of a continent?
What does agency look like in a multipolar world?

transcript.text: Kwame, the story told about Africa is usually told from somewhere else. Where do you start?
With demographics. Within a generation, roughly one in four people on Earth will be African. That’s not a footnote.
And most of them will live in cities that haven’t been built yet.
Which is a risk or an opportunity, depending on who does the building.
Agency is the word. More partners means more choices — if we negotiate as a bloc.

title: The Pragmatic Middle
dek: Resilience, not neutrality, from places asked to pick a side.
questions: Is choosing not to choose a strategy?
How long does the window stay open?

transcript.text: Layla, you’ve reported from places that are always asked to pick a side.
And they rarely want to. They want options — trade with everyone, depend on no one.
Is that neutrality?
It’s resilience. Neutrality is a posture. Resilience is a plan.
The window is real. But alignment has to become policy, or it fades.

title: The Mind Under Pressure
dek: Rituals, resets, and coaching the whole person.
questions: What is pressure, really?
Why do rituals work?

transcript.text: Priya, what is pressure, physiologically?
A signal that something matters. The trouble is when the signal gets louder than the task.
Before every match I’d tie my left boot twice. Silly, but it told my body: we’ve been here before.
That’s not silly. Rituals are a way of borrowing calm from the past.
The best coaches coach the person first. Performance follows.

title: Climate and the Long Game
dek: Ice, engineering, and institutions that can wait.
questions: How do you think in decades?
Is the long game technical or political?

transcript.text: Tomás, how do you think about time differently from the rest of us?
I study ice. Ice remembers centuries. It makes a four-year election cycle feel very short.
In the Andes we can see the change from one field season to the next.
Engineering helps with adaptation — sensors, water systems — but tools don’t decide priorities.
So the long game is a political problem, not a technical one?
It’s a patience problem. We have the knowledge. We need institutions that can wait.

title: The Next Middle:
subtitle: Why the Global Center Still Matters
dek: Amid a more polarized world, a pragmatic middle is re-emerging — not as a fence-sitting position, but as a coalition for stability, growth and agency.

glance.label: The idea
glance.text: A pragmatic global middle is gaining traction.

glance.label: Why it matters
glance.text: It could shape trade, security and the next phase of global growth.

glance.label: The bottom line
glance.text: Pragmatism, not polarity, may define the next era.

nutrition.goodFor: A clearer, big-picture read on a shifting global landscape.

bigPicture: After years of sharp divides, a more pragmatic coalition is taking shape — one that prioritizes economic resilience, national security and practical cooperation over ideology.

insights.text: From key economies in Asia to parts of Europe and the Global South, more countries are rejecting binary choices and choosing flexibility instead.
Countries are building options — on trade, technology and security — to reduce vulnerability in a more volatile world.

insights.lead: The window is real, but not endless.
insights.text: If the middle wants lasting influence, it needs to turn alignment into action, especially on economic and security cooperation.

takeaway: The middle is not a retreat from leadership — it’s a strategy for staying in the game.

title: What a Good Question Does
dek: Notes toward the book: a good question doesn’t extract an answer. It opens a room both people can stand in.

glance.label: The idea
glance.text: Questions shape the conversation more than answers do.

glance.label: Why it matters
glance.text: Most dialogue fails at the question, not the reply.

glance.label: The bottom line
glance.text: Ask what you actually want to know — then wait.

nutrition.goodFor: Anyone preparing for a conversation that matters.

bigPicture: Across every conversation on Dialoguers, the moments that open up rarely follow a clever question. They follow a specific one, asked by someone who visibly wants to know.

insights.text: People can tell within a sentence whether you are asking to learn or asking to perform.
“What did you see on the street that morning?” goes further than “What does the city mean to you?”

insights.lead: Silence is part of the question.
insights.text: The answer worth having usually arrives after the pause most interviewers fill.

takeaway: Ask the question you actually want answered — then leave room for it.

watch.text: Write the one question you most want answered.

watch.label: During
watch.text: Count to five before following up.

watch.label: After
watch.text: Note which question opened the room.
